los.text: Demonstrate the locations of the sternum, clavicle, hyoid bone, mandible and mastoid process and hence define the boundaries of the neck
los.html:
BoundaryLandmarks
UpperLower border of the mandible, mastoid process, superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance
LowerJugular (suprasternal) notch of the manubrium, clavicle, acromion, C7 spinous process
Vertebral levelLandmark
C3Hyoid
C4–5Thyroid cartilage (carotid bifurcation at its upper border)
C6Cricoid: larynx → trachea, pharynx → oesophagus
C7Vertebra prominens

los.text: Identify key spaces of cervical fascia on a cross-sectional diagram, e.g. retropharyngeal, parapharyngeal, and carotid sheath
los.html:
Fascia layerEncloses
InvestingWhole neck; splits round SCM and trapezius
PretrachealThyroid, trachea, oesophagus (visceral part); infrahyoid muscles (muscular part)
PrevertebralVertebrae, prevertebral muscles, scalenes, brachial plexus roots (continues as the axillary sheath)
Carotid sheathNeurovascular bundle; formed from all three layers
SpaceWhereClinical
RetropharyngealBehind the pharynx, in front of the prevertebral fascia (alar fascia); skull base to ~T2Retropharyngeal abscess (children): neck stiffness, drooling, stridor
Danger spaceBetween alar and prevertebral fascia; reaches the diaphragmInfection spreads to the posterior mediastinum (mediastinitis)
ParapharyngealBeside the pharynx; inverted pyramid from skull base to hyoid; contains the carotid sheathSpread from tonsils and teeth; risk to the carotid sheath

los.text: Describe the boundaries of the anterior triangle of the neck
los.html:
BoundaryFormed by
LateralAnterior border of SCM
MedialMidline of the neck
Superior (base)Lower border of the mandible
ApexJugular notch
RoofInvesting fascia, platysma
  • Subdivided by the digastric and omohyoid into submental, submandibular, carotid and muscular triangles.

los.text: Locate the carotid sheath and list its contents
los.html:
• Carotid sheath: from the skull base to the aortic arch, deep to SCM.
ContentPosition
Common / internal carotid arteryMedial
Internal jugular veinLateral
Vagus nerveBetween and behind them
Deep cervical lymph nodesAlong the IJV
  • Nearby: ansa cervicalis embedded in the front of the sheath; sympathetic trunk behind it (not inside).

los.text: Identify the surface landmarks that are used when inserting a central venous line
los.html:
Internal jugular lineat the apex of the triangle between the sternal and clavicular heads of SCM, lateral to the carotid pulse, aiming towards the same-side nipple.
Right side preferredStraight path to the SVC, lower pleural dome, avoids the thoracic duct.
Subclavian line
  • Just below the junction of the middle and medial thirds of the clavicle, aiming for the jugular notch
  • Higher pneumothorax risk.
Femoral lineMedial to the femoral artery pulse below the inguinal ligament.
TechniquePatient head-down to fill the vein and avoid air embolism; ultrasound guidance (NICE); chest X-ray afterwards (tip position, pneumothorax).

los.text: Describe the origins, courses and major branches of the common, internal and external carotid arteries
los.html:
OriginsRight CCA from the brachiocephalic trunk (behind the right sternoclavicular joint); left CCA directly from the arch.
Bifurcationat the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4) into ICA and ECA.
Carotid sinus (ICA origin, baroreceptor, CN IX) and carotid body (chemoreceptor).
ArteryCourseBranches
Internal carotidPosterolateral at first; no branches in the neck → carotid canal → cavernous sinusOphthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior and middle cerebral
External carotidAnteromedial at first; up into the parotid → splits behind the mandibular neckSuperior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary, superficial temporal ("Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students")
  • Clinical: atheroma at the bifurcation → TIA or stroke → carotid endarterectomy (risk to XII and the vagus).

Carotid pulseat the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, in the groove between the larynx and the anterior border of SCM, pressing backwards.
Cautions
  • Never press both sides at once
  • Firm pressure on the carotid sinus can cause bradycardia (carotid sinus massage is used deliberately for SVT).

los.text: Trace the paths of the vagus, accessory and hypoglossal nerves in the neck
los.html:
NervePath in the neckClinical
Vagus (X)
  • Jugular foramen → in the carotid sheath between artery and IJV → into the thorax.
  • Branches: pharyngeal, superior laryngeal (internal: sensation above the cords; external: cricothyroid), cardiac.
  • Right RLN hooks under the right subclavian artery
  • Left RLN under the arch (by the ligamentum arteriosum)
  • Both climb in the tracheo-oesophageal groove
RLN injury → hoarse voice; left RLN can be compressed by lung cancer or an aortic aneurysm
Accessory (XI)Jugular foramen → through/deep to SCM (supplies it) → crosses the posterior triangle superficially on levator scapulae → trapeziusLymph node biopsy injury → can't shrug, shoulder droops
Hypoglossal (XII)
  • Hypoglossal canal
  • → down between ICA and IJV
  • → loops forward, crossing superficial to the ICA and ECA above the hyoid
  • → floor of mouth
Tongue deviates towards the lesion; at risk in carotid endarterectomy

los.text: Compare the internal and external jugular veins and list differences between them
los.html:
Internal jugular veinExternal jugular vein
BeginsJugular foramen (continuation of the sigmoid sinus)Near the angle of the mandible (retromandibular + posterior auricular veins)
PositionDeep, in the carotid sheath under SCMSuperficial, crosses SCM under platysma
EndsJoins the subclavian vein behind the sternal end of the clavicle → brachiocephalic veinPierces deep fascia above the clavicle → subclavian vein
DrainsBrain, face, neckScalp and face (outer parts)
UseJVP (seen, not felt; double waveform), central linesVisible when distended (heart failure); peripheral access; unreliable for JVP

los.text: Name the boundaries (and floor) of the posterior triangle of the neck
los.html:
BoundaryFormed by
AnteriorPosterior border of SCM
PosteriorAnterior border of trapezius
Inferior (base)Middle third of the clavicle
ApexWhere SCM and trapezius meet on the superior nuchal line
RoofInvesting fascia
FloorPrevertebral fascia over splenius capitis, levator scapulae, scalenus medius and posterior
  • Inferior belly of omohyoid divides it into occipital and supraclavicular triangles.

los.text: Describe the relationships of the scalenus anterior muscle
los.html:
• Scalenus anterior: anterior tubercles of C3–6 transverse processes → scalene tubercle of the 1st rib.
RelationStructures
In front
  • Phrenic nerve (runs down its surface, lateral → medial, under prevertebral fascia)
  • Subclavian vein (on the 1st rib)
  • IJV
  • Transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries
BehindSubclavian artery (2nd part), brachial plexus roots and trunks (in the gap with scalenus medius), pleural dome
MedialVertebral artery, thyrocervical trunk
  • Clinical: thoracic outlet syndrome (cervical rib, tight scalenes) compresses the lower plexus and subclavian artery
    • interscalene block goes into the groove behind it (and nearly always blocks the phrenic nerve).

los.text: Locate the spinal accessory nerve within the posterior triangle, the positions of the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus, the external jugular vein and the subclavian vessels
los.html:
StructureWhere in the posterior triangle
Accessory nerveCrosses the middle superficially (just under investing fascia), from the posterior border of SCM (above its midpoint) to trapezius ~5 cm above the clavicle
Brachial plexusRoots appear between scalenus anterior and medius; trunks cross the lower part above the clavicle
External jugular veinCrosses SCM, pierces the fascia in the lower part → subclavian vein
Subclavian artery (3rd part)Lower part, on the 1st rib (pulse felt by pressing down behind the middle of the clavicle)
Subclavian veinBehind the clavicle, mostly below the triangle
OthersCervical plexus cutaneous branches (nerve point), transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries, occipital and supraclavicular nodes

los.text: Identify the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, and describe their actions and innervations
los.html:
MuscleAttachmentsActionNerveTest
SCMManubrium + medial clavicle → mastoid process and superior nuchal lineOne: tilts head to the same side, turns face to the opposite side; both: flex neck, assist breathingXI (C2–3 sensory)Turn the head against resistance (tests the opposite SCM)
TrapeziusSkull, ligamentum nuchae, C7–T12 spines → lateral clavicle, acromion, scapular spineUpper: elevates scapula (shrug); middle: retracts; lower: depresses; rotates scapula up for abduction above 90°XI (C3–4 sensory)Shrug against resistance
  • Torticollis: a short, tight SCM (birth trauma); the head tilts to the affected side and the face turns away.

los.text: Identify the cervical plexus, and note its relationship to the accessory nerve
los.html:
• Cervical plexus: anterior rami of C1–4, deep to SCM, on scalenus medius and levator scapulae.
Branch typeNerves
Cutaneous (emerge at the nerve point, midpoint of SCM's posterior border)Lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2–3), transverse cervical (C2–3), supraclavicular (C3–4)
MotorAnsa cervicalis (C1–3: infrahyoid muscles), phrenic (C3–5), branches to prevertebral muscles, scalenes, levator scapulae
Relation to XI
  • XI emerges from the posterior border of SCM just above the nerve point (the great auricular winds round SCM just below), then C3–4 branches join it on the way to trapezius.
  • In the posterior triangle, the structures below XI (plexus, vessels) lie deep under fascia
  • XI itself is superficial and easily cut.
Superficial cervical plexus blockLocal anaesthetic at the nerve point numbs the skin of the neck.

los.text: Identify the oesophagus and trachea noting their arterial supply and venous drainage
los.html:
Trachea (neck)Oesophagus (neck)
StartsC6 (below the cricoid)C6 (cricopharyngeus: narrowest point, ~15 cm from the teeth)
PositionIn front; thyroid isthmus over rings 2–4Behind the trachea, slightly to the left (surgical approach from the left)
ArteriesInferior thyroid arteriesInferior thyroid arteries
VeinsInferior thyroid veins → brachiocephalicInferior thyroid veins → brachiocephalic
  • Between them: the recurrent laryngeal nerves in the tracheo-oesophageal grooves.
Oesophagus partArteriesVeins
CervicalInferior thyroidInferior thyroid
ThoracicAortic and bronchial branchesAzygos, hemiazygos
AbdominalLeft gastricLeft gastric → portal (portosystemic anastomosis → varices)

los.text: Label a diagram or a model of the arterial trunks that arise from the arch of the aorta in the thorax
los.html:
• Arch of the aorta begins and ends at the sternal angle (T4/5).
Branch (right → left)Gives
Brachiocephalic trunkRight subclavian + right common carotid (behind the right sternoclavicular joint)
Left common carotid
Left subclavian
Subclavian branchesVertebral, internal thoracic, thyrocervical trunk, costocervical trunk, dorsal scapular.
Variants
  • "bovine arch" (brachiocephalic and left CCA share an origin)
  • Aberrant right subclavian from the end of the arch passing behind the oesophagus (dysphagia lusoria)
  • Left vertebral straight from the arch.

los.text: Label a diagram or a model of the veins that drain into the brachiocephalic veins
los.html:
• Brachiocephalic veins: IJV + subclavian vein behind each sternoclavicular joint.
    • The left is longer and crosses behind the manubrium, in front of the arch branches.
    • They join behind the right 1st costal cartilage to form the SVC.
TributarySide
Vertebral veinBoth
Internal thoracic veinBoth
Inferior thyroid veinsBoth (often the left)
Left superior intercostal veinLeft
Thymic, pericardiophrenic veinsBoth
Thoracic ductLeft venous angle (IJV–subclavian junction)
Right lymphatic ductRight venous angle
  • EJV ends in the subclavian vein, so it reaches the brachiocephalic indirectly.

los.text: Describe the lymphatic drainage of the neck (and head), identifying named lymph node collections and noting potential routes for the spread of malignant disease
los.html:
• Superficial ring at the junction of head and neck: submental, submandibular, parotid (preauricular), mastoid (retroauricular), occipital nodes.
  • All head and neck lymph ends in the deep cervical chain along the IJV
    • → jugular trunk
    • → thoracic duct (left) or right lymphatic duct.
Named nodeDrains
Jugulodigastric (angle of the mandible)Tonsil (enlarged in tonsillitis)
Jugulo-omohyoidTongue
SubmentalTip of tongue, lower lip centre, floor of mouth
SubmandibularSide of tongue, face, gums
Virchow's (left supraclavicular)Abdomen via the thoracic duct: Troisier's sign of gastric cancer
Level (neck dissection)Area
ISubmental, submandibular
II–IVUpper, middle, lower jugular
VPosterior triangle
VICentral (pre- and paratracheal): thyroid cancer
  • Spread of cancer: stepwise down the chain
    • posterior 1/3 of the tongue and midline structures drain to both sides
    • a lump in the posterior triangle suggests nasopharyngeal cancer.

los.text: Identify the phrenic nerves in the neck and recognise the consequences of surgical damage
los.html:
Phrenic nerveC3, 4, 5 ("keeps the diaphragm alive"), mainly C4.
Course
  • Forms at the upper lateral border of scalenus anterior
  • → runs down on its front (lateral → medial), under the prevertebral fascia, behind the IJV and transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries
  • → enters the thorax between the subclavian artery and vein.
SuppliesMotor to the diaphragm; sensory to the central diaphragm, pericardium and mediastinal pleura (shoulder-tip pain, C4).
DamageCauseResult
One sideNeck surgery, interscalene block, central lines, tumourRaised hemidiaphragm on CXR, paradoxical movement on sniff test, breathless lying flat
Both sidesHigh cervical cord injury (above C3), motor neurone diseaseRespiratory failure, ventilator dependence
